_howTo: Radio talks with Walla Walla. Each talk has turns; in each turn Walla Walla says "them" and the player picks one of up to three "replies". A reply can have a "back" line, and "right": true marks the right answer to a question (it is never scored). Every reply leads on to the next turn. "cue" is when the talk comes on: "start" as the lesson opens, {"after": "<figure>"} once that figure's task is done, or "check" as the final check opens. "locals" names who in town asked a forecast question, by the forecast's "id" in the lesson file.

turns.them: Harrow, Walla Walla, right on the sked. How was your first week? Anybody knock on the door yet?

replies.back: The goat is Ole Haugen’s. It goes wherever Ole goes, and it judges you. Don’t take it personally.

replies.say: Ole Haugen came by. And Hap Delaney from the airfield.
replies.back: The two finest worriers in Adams County. Ole frets about his hay. Hap frets about nothing, which is worse.

turns.them: Let me guess. Ole has hay cut and lying in the field, and he wants to know if those little puffy clouds every morning mean rain. And Hap wants to know when the morning fog will let him off the ground.

replies.back: Because it’s June, and they ask me the same thing every June. I’m passing them on to you, with my compliments.
Thirty years of guesses. They stop being luck after the first twenty.

turns.them: And what did you tell them?

replies.say: “Probably not” to Ole and “later” to Hap.
replies.back: A politician’s answer. Accurate and useless.

replies.say: That I’d get back to them.
replies.back: Wise. A tenderfoot who admits not knowing is worth two who guess.
Don’t you dare. That knee belongs to the family.

turns.them: Here’s tonight’s homework. Before you can answer either of them, you have to know what a cloud actually is, and it isn’t what you think. We’ll start with Hap’s fog, because fog is the simplest cloud there is. Ole’s puffy clouds can wait a week; tell him to keep his eye on them. Read the lesson, play with the jar, and call me back when you know why the valley fills with fog.

replies.back: Read the lesson. I’m not doing your homework for you. Well, maybe a little, later.

turns.them: Harrow, still there? Quick quiz while the coffee’s hot. You’ve got your jar of air at 20 degrees, and you add more water vapour to it. Does its dew point go up or down?

replies.back: Right. More vapour, more crowding, so it takes less cooling before the molecules start to stick. That’s why a muggy evening fogs up a cold milk can so fast.
Other way round. More vapour means the molecules are more crowded, so they start sticking sooner. The dew point goes up.
That’s the trap. The dew point depends on how much vapour there is, not on how warm the air happens to be. Add vapour, and up it goes.

turns.them: Try this. On a warm afternoon, fill a glass with cold water from the well and watch it sweat. The glass is a little patch of cold ground, and the air touching it just went past its dew point.

replies.say: So that’s where dew comes from.
replies.back: Same trick, done by the whole valley floor overnight.
Lemonade works. Edna Pruitt’s lemonade works better, but don’t tell her I said so.

turns.them: Now, about Hap’s fog. What kind of night makes fog by dawn?

replies.back: That’s it. A clear sky lets the ground lose its heat, no wind leaves the chilled air lying on the ground, and damp air has its dew point close by.
Backwards. Cloud keeps the ground warm like a blanket, and wind stirs the cold air away. Clear, still and damp is the recipe.
Damp helps, but a cloudy or breezy night after rain stays clear at the ground. You need clear and still as well.

turns.them: Hap will try to fly through it anyway. Last spring he landed in the Kessler place’s turnip field and called it a “precautionary arrival.”

replies.back: Hap is always all right. The turnips were not.

turns.them: Every blanket called, and not one heap mistaken for one. The fellows at the radio club will be pleased you got through their photographs. Now earn your keep: Hap is waiting on his answer.

replies.back: Every telephone in Harrow goes through Mabel at the switchboard, and Mabel can’t keep a secret. Do it yourself.

locals.dawn-fog: Hap Delaney, who flies the mail out of Harrow Field at first light, asks:
